parole.testo: From a Turkic language (possibly Chagatai), ultimately from Proto-Common Turkic *apa (“mother, elder sister, aunt”). Compare Uzbek oba, Kazakh апа (apa), and Azerbaijani aba.

From a Turkic language (possibly Chagatai), ultimately from Proto-Turkic *eke. Compare Kazakh әже (äje, “grandmother”), Chagatai اچه (äçä, “mother, old woman”), Turkmen eje (“mother, aunt, elder sister”).
Borrowed from Turkic, from Proto-Turkic *arpa. Compare Azerbaijani arpa.
Borrowed from Turkic, Ottoman Turkish آغز (ağız), ultimately Proto-Turkic *aguŕ.
Borrowed from a Turkic language. Compare Turkish açmaz (“pinned (chess)”).
Derived from Turkic. Compare Uzbek aya, oyi, and Turkic-derived kinship terms in other Persian dialects like Hazaragi آبَه (āba).
From a Turkic language.
A Turkic borrowing. Compare Azerbaijani otaq, Turkish otağ (Ottoman Turkish اوتاق (otak)), Turkmen otag, Turkish oda (Ottoman Turkish اوطه (oda)), all meaning chamber, room.
From Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani oturaq.
From a Turkic source, such as Ottoman Turkish اوتو (ütü), Azerbaijani ütü, Turkmen ütük. Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ütüg.
A Turkic borrowing which displaced the native formation دیگدان (dêgdân, “stove”) in Iranian Persian. Compare Azerbaijani ocaq, Ottoman Turkish اوجاق (ocak).
Borrowed from Turkic, from the same source as Turkish araba. See there for more.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani ördək, Kyrgyz өрдөк (ördök), Tatar ürdäk, Turkish ördek. Early attestations are from the 1500s.
From a Turkic language.
Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately a derivation of Proto-Turkic *ar- (“gift”). Compare Azerbaijani armağan, Turkish armağan, Uyghur ئارماغان (armaghan), Uzbek armugʻon.
From Turkic. Compare Kyrgyz өрүк (örük), Turkish erik, Turkmen erik.
From Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani ulaq, Chagatai اولاغ (ulaǧ), Uyghur ئۇلاغ (ulagh), ئۇلاق (ulaq), Uzbek uloq, ulov, Ottoman Turkish اولاق (ulak), Turkmen ulag.
A Turkic borrowing, compare Azerbaijani alov, Uzbek olov, Turkish alev, Kazakh алау (alaw).
From a Turkic source, possibly Azerbaijani ülgü (“pattern”). Compare with Turkish ülgü, Turkmen ülňi, Kyrgyz үлгү (ülgü), Kazakh үлгі (ülgi), Chuvash ӗлкӗ (ĕlk̬ĕ), Bashkir өлгө (ölgö), etc.

parole.significato: A small round piece of dough; a soup made of this
parole.testo: A Turkic borrowing: compare Old Anatolian Turkish اوماج (omac), Ottoman Turkish اوماج (omac), Turkish omaç, Azerbaijani umac, all referring to a kind of dish.
From a Turkic source. Compare Uyghur ئۈگرە (ügre) and Uzbek ugra.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Ottoman Turkish آیاغ (ayag, “drinking cup”).
From a Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ēl.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Ottoman Turkish ایلغار (ılgar), Azerbaijani ilğar, Uzbek ilgʻor, Uyghur ئىلغار (ilghar).
Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ēlči, from *ēl (“realm, country”) + *-či (profession suffix).
Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *batgak. Compare Ottoman Turkish باتاق (batak), Turkish batak, and Tatar batqaq.
Borrowed from Turkic, compare Turkish bacı.
Borrowed from Turkic, Turkish bağa.

parole.significato: escort, company (sending someone off on the road)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *badrak (“banner, flag”) which escorts the convoy. Doublet of بیرق (bayraq /beyraġ).
From Turkic. Compare Turkish börk.
Borrowed from a Turkic source, from Proto-Turkic *buka.
Borrowed from a Turkic source, from Proto-Turkic *bāka. Doublet of باخه (bāxa /bâxe, “tortoise”).

Borrowed from Turkic, likely from Ottoman Turkish بلدرجین (bıldırcın) or Azerbaijani bildirçin, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bïldur-, *buldïr- (“quail”). Largely displaced Classical Persian وَرْتِیج (wartīj) in Iranian Persian.
Borrowed from Turkic.
Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bilegü.
Borrowed from a Turkic language.: compare Azerbaijani boran.
Probably from Turkic بوش (boş, “loose, untethered”).
Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *badrak. See Azerbaijani bayraq, Turkish bayrak, and Uzbek bayroq.

parole.significato: beylerbey or beglarbegi, a medieval and early modern title:
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Ottoman Turkish بكلر بكی (beyler beyi, literally “bey of beys”).
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani dağ, Turkish dağ, Uzbek togʻ.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Karakhanid تُتُغ (tutuğ), تُتُق (tutuq, “curtain”), Turkmen tuty (“curtain”). Early attestations include Anvārī (1100s).
From a Turkic source, from Proto-Turkic *tokïmak. Compare Azerbaijani toxmaq, Chagatai توخماق (twxmʾq /⁠toxmaq⁠/).

From Turkic, see Ottoman Turkish تورپ (turp). Intuited shakily by Laufer by Doerfer and Clauson to be an Iranian borrowing in Turkic, in view of internal etymological opacity of the term in Turkic and the Persian variant turf, which we reckon to be a secondary variant like شفدر (šafdar) for شبدر (ša

parole.significato: free, exempted from tribute or taxes, not amenable to punishment
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Turkic descendant of Proto-Turkic *tarkan.

parole.significato: Turkmen (member of one of various Turkic ethnic groups in Central and West Asia)
parole.testo: From a Turkic language, combining Old Turkic 𐱅𐰇𐰼𐰜 (t²ẅr²ẅk², “Turk”) with a suffix *-man sometimes found in tribal and place names, cf. Old Anatolian Turkish قرامان (qarâmân, Turkic dynasty in southern Anatolia) from قرا (qarâ, “black”), or Old Turkic 𐰚𐰇𐰏𐰢𐰤 (k²ẅg²mn², “Sayan Mountains”) from 𐰚𐰇𐰚 (k²
A Turkic borrowing. Compare Ottoman Turkish تاصمه (tasma).
From Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani döşək.
From a Turkic language. Akin to Tajik тағо (taġo).
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Chagatai تالاشماق (talaşmaq, “to compete”) and Ottoman Turkish طالاشمق (dalaşmak, “to quarrel”).
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani dəmir, Crimean Tatar temir, Tatar timer, Turkish demir.
Borrowed from Turkic. See Ottoman Turkish توتون (tütün) above.
From a Turkic language, from Proto-Common Turkic *tor. Cognate with Old Turkic [script needed] (tor, “net”), Southern Altai тор (tor, “net”), Azerbaijani tor (“net”).
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Turkish döşek.
From Turkic. Compare Turkish top.
Borrowed from Turkic; attested since Farrukhī Sīstānī, early 11th century, in the sense of "slap." The sense of "pistol" is also a semantic loan from Ottoman Turkish طبانجه (tabanca, “pistol”).
A Turkic borrowing, compare Turkish topal (“lame; shorter in one leg”), from top (“round thing”).
From a Turkic source, such as Azerbaijani təpə, Uzbek tepa, Ottoman Turkish تپه (tepe). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *tepe.
From a Turkic language. Compare Uyghur تۈگمە (tügme), Uzbek tugma.
From Turkic.
Borrowed from a Turkic source, from Middle Mongol ᠵᠠᠷ (ǰar). Not related to Arabic جَهْر (jahr).
From Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani carçı, Ottoman Turkish جارجی (carcı), Turkmen jarçy, Uyghur جارچى (jarchi), Uzbek jarchi. Analyzable as جار (jār /jâr) + ـچی (-čī /-či).
From Turkic, compare Ottoman Turkish چیش (čiš, “urine”), from Proto-Common Turkic *čiš.

parole.significato: one side of the die known in English as knucklebone, jackstone or astragal
parole.testo: A Turkic borrowing, compare Azerbaijani çıqqıltı (“click”).

parole.significato: Sir, Mister; a title attached after the name of a man, marking politeness and/or social distance.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic; first attested in Islamic lands in Karakhanid coinage from the 900s. See Old Turkic 𐰴𐰍𐰣 (k¹g¹n¹ /⁠qaɣan⁠/) for more.
Borrowed from Turkic languages. Compare Old Anatolian Turkish خانم (ḫānum), Chagatai خانِم (xānım).
Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kaŕgan.
Possibly borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kadïŋ (“birch”).
Apparently a Turkic borrowing. Compare Ottoman Turkish قاو (kav) / Azerbaijani qov (“tinder”) and خاو (hav, “fuzz, down”) / xov (“nap, pile”).
Borrowed from Turkic, compare Azerbaijani dədə, Uyghur دادا (dada), Turkish dede, English dad, Russian дед (ded, “dad”).
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani qardaş, Turkish dadaş (eastern dialectal), Turkish kardeş, Gagauz kardaş.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Turkmen daýza and Turkish teyze.
A Turkic borrowing: compare Turkish dayı, Azerbaijani dayı.
From a Turkic source, such as Azerbaijani durna, Chagatai ترنا (turna), Ottoman Turkish طورنه (turna). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *turńa.
Borrowed from Turkic, cf. Azerbaijani dolma, Turkish dolma.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Turkish döşek.

parole.significato: twin (two people born from the same uterus)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Abyanehi دوقول (döqūl), Ashtiani دولغی (doloγī), Shushtari دغلی (doġolī).
From a Turkic language. Compare Ottoman Turkish دوگمه (düğme), Azerbaijani düymə, Turkmen düwme.
A Turkic borrowing, see Turkish sac / ساج.
From a Turkic source. Compare Azerbaijani soraq, Ottoman Turkish صوروق (soruk), Chagatai سوراغ (soraǧ), Uzbek soʻroq, Kazakh сұрақ (suraq).
From Turkic, Proto-Turkic *sakïŕ (“gum, resin”).
Borrowed from Turkic.

parole.testo: Because of the measure a likely Turkic or Mongolic borrowing but the root is uncertain, first attested in both Persian and Ottoman Turkish in the 17th century, perhaps from Azerbaijani sür (“to drive, to push, to send”) + sat (“to sell”), for contributions may involve forced sales or “sales” for fre
A Turkic *su-silən (literally “water-scrubbing”) as also other languages denote the bird after its tail movements.
Derived from Turkic or Mongolic; Although it is referred to as a Khwarezmian term in the Indian edition of Burhan-i Qati.
From a Turkic source, despite Clauson; ultimately from Proto-Turkic *sekü.
From a Turkic source, ultimately from Persian شیرین (šīrīn /širin, “sweet”) and a descendant of Proto-Turkic *bïyan. Compare Azerbaijani şirinbiyan, Uzbek shirinmiya.
Borrowed from Turkic. Attested since Seljuk times in the eleventh century.
A Turkic borrowing: compare Chagatai غاز (ğaz), Ottoman Turkish قاز (qaz), Azerbaijani qaz. Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kāŕ.

The Turkic *kiān (“blood”) as in Kazakh қандыағаш (qandıağaš, “alder”). Analogously, for cornel, *kïŕïl (“red”) also sufficed alone for a dendronym in East Slavic, Russian кизи́л (kizíl), Ukrainian кизи́л (kyzýl), Belarusian кізі́л (kizíl), in spite of Turkic languages themselves only using derivati
Borrowed from Turkic, from Proto-Turkic *-či. Compare Azerbaijani -çi, Ottoman Turkish ـجی (-ci).

Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kāplama. Compare Ottoman Turkish قاپلامه (kaplama, “covering”), Azerbaijani qablama (“packaging; pot”), Uzbek qoplama (“covering”). Northern Luri غۋڵںمںە (qüłəmə).
Borrowed from Turkic, probably Azerbaijani qat- (“to add, to mix in”).

Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani qatır, Turkish katır, Kazakh қашыр (qašır), Uzbek xachir, Uyghur خېچىر (xëchir) etc. Related to Tajik хачир (xačir), which is also from the same Proto-Turkic etymon through the borrowing of Mongolian [Term?] into a Turkic language.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Turkish kat- (“to add, to mix”), Azerbaijani qat- (“to add, to mix in”), etc.
Borrowed from a Turkic language.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani qayıq, Kazakh қайық (qayıq), Turkish kayık, Turkmen gaýyk.
Of Turkic origin. Compare Azerbaijani qışlaq, Turkish kışlak, Kazakh қыстау (qıstaw), etc...
From Turkic. Compare Turkish koşun, Azerbaijani qoşun, Uyghur قوشۇن (qoshun), Turkmen goşun, Uzbek qoʻshin, Kazakh қосын (qosın), etc.
A Turkic borrowing, see Old Anatolian Turkish قلاغوز (qulağuz, qulavuz). Compare also Khwarezmian خلاور (xlʾwr, “guide”) (< ? earlier *xlʾwz).

Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Turkish kurbağa (“frog”), Azerbaijani qurbağa (“frog”), Uzbek qurbaqa (“frog”). Largely displaced Iranian terms for "frog" such as وک (vak), inherited from Middle Persian, and غوک (ġuk) and چغز (čaġz), both from Sogdian.
From a Turkic language, from Proto-Turkic *kuĺ (“bird”), cognate to Ottoman Turkish قوش (kuş), Old Turkic 𐰴𐰆𐰽 (k¹ws¹), Azerbaijani quş, etc.

parole.significato: kaymak (a creamy dairy product, similar to clotted cream, made in the Balkans, Turkey, the Middle East, Central Asia, I…
parole.testo: Derived from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kańak. Compare with Azerbaijani qaymaq, Turkish kaymak, or Kazakh қаймақ (qaymaq).
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Ottoman Turkish قیمه, قییمه (modern Turkish kıyma).
From a Turkic source: compare Turkish kıyın, Turkmen kyn, Uzbek qiyin.

Via some Turkic source, compare Azerbaijani nökər (“servant”), Turkmen nöker, Uzbek navkar. Ultimately from Middle Mongol ᠨᠥᠬᠦᠷ (nökür /⁠nökör⁠/), from Proto-Mongolic *nökör (“friend”). Compare Modern Mongolian нөхөр (nöxör, “friend”). The meaning of “servant” is owing to a semantic shift that happe
From a Turkic source. Compare Turkish pars. Doublet of پلنگ (palang).
A Turkic borrowing. Compare Uzbek parma. Possibly from the same etymon or related to Ottoman Turkish بورغو (burgu, “drill”). Unrelated to similar Semitic words treated at Arabic بَيْرَم (bayram).
From a Turkic source, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *bïčak.

Doublet of چاغ (čâġ) and from the same Turkic source as the former. The semantic development must have been along the lines of 'measure of something' → 'in high measure' → 'strong' → 'thick, healthy, sound' etc. Compare Uzbek chogʻ (“happy, gay, joyful”), Azerbaijani çağ (“healthy; well-fed; happy”)
Apparently from the Turkic چاولی (çavli) in reminiscence to the front of a sparrowhawk or like bird. Compare Uzbek chovli (“skimmer”).

A Turkic borrowing: compare Old Anatolian Turkish چپار / چاپار / چپر (çapar), Ottoman Turkish چاپار (çapar), Azerbaijani çapar. Ultimately from the root underlying Ottoman Turkish چاپمق (çapmak), Azerbaijani çapmaq. Also from Turkic (directly or via Persian): Middle Armenian չափառ (čʻapʻaṙ), Armenia
From a Turkic source. Compare Azerbaijani çapmaq (“to plunder”).
From a Turkic language, compare چبوق (çubuk, çıbuk, çibuk) above.
Probably from a Turkic source, if the relation is not in the opposite direction. Compare Russian чугун (čugun).
From Turkic. Compare Azerbaijani çörək, Turkish çörek and Turkmen çörek.
From Turkic. Compare Turkish çörekçi.

Related to چمیدن (čamīdan /čamidan, “to stroll, saunter”) and Old Armenian ճեմ (čem, “walk”), an Iranian borrowing. The senses "lawn" and "meadow" are borrowed from a Turkic source, such as Turkish çimen (“meadow”), Azerbaijani çəmən (“meadow”), Turkmen çemen (“meadow; bundle, bouquet”), Uzbek chama

Turkic borrowing. Found in Kazakh шөміш (šömiš), Kyrgyz чөмүч (cömüc), Bashkir сүмес (sümes), Uzbek choʻmich, Chagatai [script needed] (čömüš), and compare probably separate but similarly formed Uyghur [script needed] (qemič), Karakhanid [script needed] (qamɨč), Tuvan хымыш (xımış), Yakut хомуос (xo
Turkic borrowing, from Proto-Turkic *kagun (“melon”).
Probably from Turkic.
A Turkic borrowing, equivalent to Ottoman Turkish كورك (kürk, “fur”).
Unknown; possibly borrowed from Turkic, as the green, seedless variety used is said to originate in Bokhara, Uzbekistan. Compare Azerbaijani kişmiş (“raisin”).
From a Turkic source, from Proto-Turkic *kēne (“tick”).

parole.significato: council; assembly; consultation; meeting for advice
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *keŋe- (“to advise”).

parole.significato: migration (originally of nomadic tribes, now generally)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic, from Proto-Turkic *köč- (“nomadizing”). Compare Chagatai كوچ (köç), Azerbaijani köç, Turkish göç. Already attested as the name of a nomadic tribe in the Shāhnāma, c. 1010.
A Turkic borrowing. Compare Azerbaijani kəpək.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Ottoman Turkish یاتاق (yatak), Azerbaijani yataq.
A Turkic borrowing, compare Turkish yara (“wound”).
Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yagï (“enemy”). Early attestations include The Alchemy of Happiness, from the early 1100s.
Borrowed from Turkic, compare Ottoman Turkish یدك.
From a Turkic source, compare Azerbaijani yaraq, Turkish yarak, Chagatai یاراغ (yarağ).
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Turkish yürekli, Azerbaijani ürəkli. This word ultimately goes back to Proto-Turkic *yürek (“heart”).

Borrowed from Turkic, probably from Proto-Turkic *yag- (“to fall from the sky (of rain, snow, etc.)”) with a figurative sense of "to fall upon, to attack, to raid", which then transferred to "the outcome of a raid; booty, pillage". Compare Turkish yağma (“raiding, looting; sack, pillage”). Attested

From a Turkic source, from Proto-Turkic *yaka (“edge; collar”). Compare Turkish yaka (“collar”), Azerbaijani yaxa (“collar”), Uzbek yoqa (“collar; side; bank”), Uyghur ياقا (yaqa, “collar; side; bank”).

parole.significato: only used in ینگه دنیا (yenge donyâ, “the New World, America”).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Turkic, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yaŋï (“new”).
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Turkish yavaş and Azerbaijani yavaş.
Borrowed from Turkic. Compare Turkish yavaş yavaş.
A Turkic borrowing, from Chagatai یورش (yöriš, yörüš, yürüš).
Borrowed from Turkic.

parole.significato: countryside area where people go to escape the summer heat
parole.testo: Of Turkic origin. Compare Azerbaijani yaylaq, Turkish yaylak, Uzbek yaylov, Kazakh жайлау (jaylaw), etc...

Perhaps from a Turkic language, see Proto-Common Turkic *aš, however there seems to be an unexplained mismatch in vowel length. Compare Azerbaijani aş, Bashkir аш (aş), Yakut ас (as). Alternatively, inherited from Middle Persian [Term?] (/⁠āš⁠/), a hapax legomenon found in the Vendidad, although thi

Ultimately a derivative of Proto-Iranian *gauz- (“to hide, conceal”), compare Sanskrit गूहति (gūhati). Possibly influenced by Northeastern Iranian, compare Sogdian [script needed] (ʾʾγʾwδ /⁠āγōδ⁠/, “cover, shelter, barn”). Alternatively, borrowed from a Turkic source: cognate with Ottoman Turkish آغ
Probably from Middle Iranian, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰoh₁ro- (“gap, empty space”). Alternatively from Turkic (compare Turkish yar).

Inherited from Middle Persian HLYA (/⁠sik⁠/), [Term?] (/⁠sarkāw⁠/). Alternatively, borrowed from Turkic, compare Azerbaijani sirkə, Ottoman Turkish سركه (sirke), etc. According to Doerfer, direction of a possible borrowing between Iranian and Turkic is not clear.

From a Turkic source, such as Chagatai قوتاس (qotas), Azerbaijani qotaz, Ottoman Turkish خوطاز (hotaz); ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kotuŕ (“yak”). Alternatively, lexicographer Mohammad Moin marked it as the Arabicised form of an unspecified Greek term.

From کاو (kâv, present stem of کاویدن (kâvidan, “to burrow, to dig, to search deeply, to investigate”)) + ـاک (-âk, suffix that forms the active participle from the present verb stem).
